What's next?
The avatar is built with VRCFury, which means it's modular - parts can be added, removed, and swapped out without needing to know 3D. Most of it is just dragging a prefab into Unity and re-uploading.

Add-ons are modular pieces you can attach to your avatar in Unity. The process is the same for all of them - drag a prefab onto the avatar root in the Hierarchy and re-upload. VRCFury wires up the toggle in your expression menu automatically.

If you want to change how the avatar looks beyond what the in-game color controls offer - like swapping a texture file entirely or adjusting the emission and roughness - you'll do that by editing the material directly in Unity.

If you'd rather paint textures flat in a 2D image editor than work directly on the 3D model, this is the approach for you. You edit the texture as a regular image file, export it, and drop it into Unity.

Adobe Substance Painter lets you paint textures directly onto the 3D model, which makes it much easier to paint across seams and see exactly how your work looks on the avatar. It's the more capable option compared to flat 2D editing, but has a steeper learning curve.

The avatar is built with VRCFury, which means it's modular - parts can be added, removed, and swapped out without needing to know 3D. Most of it is just dragging a prefab into Unity and re-uploading.

I want to add an outfit, hair style, or system - Go to Add-ons. The process is the same for all of them. I want to repaint or retexture the avatar - You have two routes depending on what software you use: Substance Painter for 3D texture painting directly on the model PSD & 2D Editing if you prefer working flat in an image editor like Photoshop or Clip Studio Paint I want to apply a new texture I made - Materials & Textures covers swapping textures in Unity. I just uploaded - what's already in my radial menu? - Everything is set up automatically on upload. Check the Systems section for what's included out of the box.

Add-ons are modular pieces you can attach to your avatar in Unity. The process is the same for all of them - drag a prefab onto the avatar root in the Hierarchy and re-upload. VRCFury wires up the toggle in your expression menu automatically.

The avatar includes five outfits. Find them in Monado_Art/Lucario ReUnited VRC/Add-ons/Outfits/. Outfit Concert Martial Arts Ruins Sir Aaron Space Jacket Navigate to the outfit folder in the Project panel Drag the prefab onto the top-level avatar object in the Hierarchy Re-upload - see Uploading if you need a refresher tip To remove an outfit, delete its prefab from the Hierarchy and re-upload.

Appearance options for hair, head shape, face style, and body. Find them in Monado_Art/Lucario ReUnited VRC/Add-ons/Trait/. Folder What it changes Hair Hair style Head Head shape Face Styles Facial appearance Body Body shape Same process as outfits - drag the prefab onto the avatar root and re-upload. tip These don't conflict with each other. You can add one from each folder at the same time.

The avatar ships with these systems built in and ready to use from the expression menu: System What it does GoGo Loco Fly, prone, and crouch locomotion modes Face Tracking Custom face tracking for supported headsets Facial Expressions Hand gesture-driven expressions Color Customization Basic in-game color controls Eye Proximity Reacts when other players get close to your face Hair Flip X Hair physics and wiggle controls Nose End Indicator Shows nose tip position for face tracking alignment Tail Control Manual control over tail physics FUCK Eyes pop out when you talk loud GoGo Loco and Face Tracking are modified external packages and sit directly in Add-ons/ rather than Add-ons/System/. The rest are in Add-ons/System/. If you removed a system and want it back, drag its prefab back onto the avatar root and re-upload. warning TODO - add screenshots or video of the drag-and-drop process

If you want to change how the avatar looks beyond what the in-game color controls offer - like swapping a texture file entirely or adjusting the emission and roughness - you'll do that by editing the material directly in Unity.

A texture is an image file - like a PNG - that gets painted onto the 3D model. A material is the full set of settings that controls how a surface looks: which textures it uses, how shiny it is, whether it glows, and so on. The avatar body uses a single material, so there's one place to change all of this.
documents.s: What's a material, what's a texture?

documents.t: In the Project panel, navigate to Monado_Art/Lucario ReUnited VRC/Materials/ Click the body material to select it The Inspector will show all of its properties on the right

Slot What it controls Base Color / Albedo The main painted texture Normal Map Surface detail like bumps and creases - usually leave this alone Emission Glow - color and texture of any glowing areas Metallic / Roughness How shiny or matte the surface looks

Drag your new texture file from the Project panel into the slot in the Inspector. Click the small thumbnail to the left of the slot name and it'll highlight - then drag your file onto it. tip Press Ctrl+S to save after making changes, then re-upload to see them in VRChat. warning TODO - add screenshots of the material Inspector and slots

If you'd rather paint textures flat in a 2D image editor than work directly on the 3D model, this is the approach for you. You edit the texture as a regular image file, export it, and drop it into Unity.

Different 2D apps use different native file formats. The avatar textures are provided as PSD files, which most apps can open. Format App Notes .psd Adobe Photoshop Industry standard. Readable by most other apps .csp Clip Studio Paint Popular for illustration. Has a one-time purchase option .mdp MediBang Paint Free and lightweight. Good starting point tip Work in your app's native format and only export to PNG when you're ready to bring it into Unity. Editing a flattened PNG loses your layers.

The avatar's texture files are in your Unity project under Monado_Art/Lucario ReUnited VRC/Textures/. Right-click the file in the Project panel and choose Show in Explorer to open its location on disk, then open it in your image editor from there.

The texture is a flat image that wraps around the 3D model. The way it maps to the model is determined by the UV layout - essentially a flattened-out version of the mesh. If your app supports it, import the UV layout as a reference layer so you know what part of the image corresponds to what part of the model. This prevents painting in the wrong spot. info TODO - add UV layout image for reference

Keep your original texture on its own locked layer at the bottom and do all your painting above it. This way you can always revert to the original without starting over. Common layer setup: Original - locked, untouched base texture Edits - your changes on top UV Guide - the UV layout for reference, set to Multiply or low opacity

When you're done, export a flattened copy as PNG. Avoid JPEG - it introduces compression artifacts that look bad on a 3D model, especially near sharp edges. In most apps: File → Export As → PNG, make sure it's the same resolution as the original texture.

Drop the exported PNG into your Unity project (drag it into the Project panel or copy it into the project folder). Then open the material and drag the new texture into the relevant slot - see Materials & Textures for how to do that. tip Press Ctrl+S in Unity after swapping the texture, then re-upload to see it in VRChat.

Resolution - Export at the same resolution as the original texture. Scaling up causes blurring, scaling down loses detail. Color space - Body/diffuse textures should be in sRGB. If colors look washed out or wrong in Unity, check that the texture import settings have sRGB (Color Texture) checked. Normal maps - If you're editing the normal map, it needs to stay in linear color space. Don't apply color profiles or corrections to it.

Adobe Substance Painter lets you paint textures directly onto the 3D model, which makes it much easier to paint across seams and see exactly how your work looks on the avatar. It's the more capable option compared to flat 2D editing, but has a steeper learning curve. For a quick start, check out this introduction video and this beginner playlist.

The ## above is what every ## heading looks like automatically - no import needed. The XenoMarkers components give explicit control over the same shapes. SectionTab SectionBanner SubSectionBanner ### Subsection Name <SubSectionBanner /> GaugeHeaderright value

Most of the time ## headings are all you need. Use the explicit components when you need a tab label above a banner, a named sub-section break, or a gauge bar with a right-side value: import { SectionTab, SectionBanner, SubSectionBanner, GaugeHeader } from '@site/src/components/XenoMarkers'; <SectionTab>Optional</SectionTab> <SectionBanner>My Section</SectionBanner> ### Named Break <SubSectionBanner /> <GaugeHeader value="3/3">Progress Header</GaugeHeader>

Every component accepts a size prop that sets its font-size. All internal dimensions use em units so everything scales proportionally: <SectionBanner size="0.8rem">Smaller than default</SectionBanner> <SectionBanner size="1.5rem">Bigger than default</SectionBanner> <GaugeHeader size="1rem" value="done">Larger gauge</GaugeHeader> Default sizes: SectionTab → 0.72rem, SectionBanner → 1rem, SubSectionBanner → 1.25rem, GaugeHeader → 0.78rem.

The table of contents only picks up markdown ## headings - JSX components are invisible to it. If a section using an explicit component also needs a ToC entry, place a ## heading immediately before it: ## My Section <SectionBanner>My Section</SectionBanner> The CSS collapses the ## heading visually (the component shows instead) while keeping the anchor alive for the ToC link.
All card components share a dark frame with metallic-yellow rivets at each corner.

Settings Shows a screenshot inside the card frame with an optional floating pill label above it. src is passed through useBaseUrl automatically - use the /img/ path as-is. import { LocationCard } from '@site/src/components/LocationCard'; <LocationCard src="/img/settings-panel.png" title="Settings" /> <LocationCard src="/img/something.png" /> {/* no label */} The highlight prop annotates regions of the screenshot. Coordinates are fractions of the image (0–1). Highlighted regions pulse with a gold border; hovering fades them so the full image is visible. grow expands a region outward by that many pixels on every side: <LocationCard src="/img/panel.png" title="Panel" highlight={[ { l: 0.05, t: 0.1, w: 0.4, h: 0.15, text: "Name field" }, { l: 0.6, t: 0.7, w: 0.3, h: 0.2, text: "Save button", grow: 4 }, ]} />

⚠️Put a screenshot of the right-click menu here Right-click Menu Same frame and rivets as LocationCard, but shows a caution area instead of an image. Use it anywhere a screenshot is still needed and replace the whole tag with a <LocationCard> once the real image is ready. import { PlaceholderCard } from '@site/src/components/PlaceholderCard'; <PlaceholderCard title="Settings Panel" text="Put a screenshot of the Settings panel here" />

Anything here gets the riveted frame. Custom Content The raw frame primitive used by LocationCard and PlaceholderCard. Use it directly when you need the riveted frame around non-image content. Accepts title, style, className, frameClassName, labelClassName, frameStyle, labelStyle, and topSpacing="none" to suppress the margin reserved for the floating label. import { XenoCardFrame } from '@site/src/components/XenoCardFrame';

Anything here gets the riveted frame.

Never hardcode hex or rgb values anywhere in CSS or JSX. Always reference the --xeno-* CSS variables defined in src/css/custom.css.

Centers a short intro sentence directly under the page h1. Collapses its own bottom margin so it sits tight against whatever follows. import { DocsPageLead } from '@site/src/components/DocsPageLead'; # My Page <DocsPageLead>A one-liner that describes what this page is for.</DocsPageLead> ## First Section

Two-column layout: text on the left, a media card on the right. Stacks vertically on narrow viewports with the media below. The media prop takes any JSX, typically a <LocationCard /> or <HoverVideo />. import { DocsMediaRow } from '@site/src/components/DocsMediaRow'; <DocsMediaRow media={<LocationCard src="/img/something.png" title="The Panel" />}> Your step-by-step instructions here. The media card floats right at 220 px wide and aligns to the bottom of the text column. </DocsMediaRow>

Hover-aware wrapper for optional steps that have an accompanying video. Hovering the <HoverOption> block adds a warm left accent bar and plays the embedded <HoverVideo>. Omit src from <HoverVideo> to show a "Video coming soon" placeholder instead. import { HoverOption, HoverVideo } from '@site/src/components/HoverOption'; <HoverOption> <DocsMediaRow media={<HoverVideo src="/video/my-option.mp4" title="Right-click Menu" />}> 1. Your steps here... </DocsMediaRow> </HoverOption> The hover effect degrades gracefully to plain content if JS is unavailable.

These render inline replicas of VCC's own UI so prose instructions match what the reader sees. Import what you need: import { VccIcon, VccProjectsLabel, VccManageProjectLabel, AddIcon, RemoveIcon, VersionNone, VersionInstalled, } from '@site/src/components/InstallationInlineUi/InstallationInlineUi'; <VccIcon /> - the VCC favicon inline with text. Accepts a size prop (CSS value, default 1.2em). Open Creator Companion. Open <VccIcon /> **Creator Companion**. <VccProjectsLabel /> - the Projects sidebar entry as it appears in VCC, including the grid icon. Go to the Projects tab. Go to the <VccProjectsLabel /> tab. <VccManageProjectLabel /> - the Manage Project action label, styled like a small VCC button. Click Manage Project next to your project. Click <VccManageProjectLabel /> next to your project. <AddIcon /> and <RemoveIcon /> - the circular add and remove buttons from VCC's package list. Click to install, to remove. Click <AddIcon /> to install, <RemoveIcon /> to remove. <VersionNone /> and <VersionInstalled /> - the version dropdown pills from the VCC package list. If the version column shows none, the package isn't installed. Once installed it shows 1.2.3. If the version column shows <VersionNone />, the package isn't installed. Once installed it shows <VersionInstalled />.

Small inline icons matching the Unity editor's own file-type indicators. Use them next to any mention of a Unity asset type. import { SceneIcon, PrefabIcon, ModelIcon, PrefabModelIcon, PrefabVariantIcon, UnityPackageIcon, UnityPackage } from '@site/src/components/UnityIcon'; <SceneIcon /> <PrefabIcon /> <ModelIcon /> <PrefabModelIcon /> <PrefabVariantIcon /> <UnityPackageIcon /> Save your .unitypackage file somewhere you can find it. All icon components accept an optional size prop (number, pixels). Default is 16. Double-click the scene file <SceneIcon /> to open it. Drag the prefab <PrefabIcon /> into the Hierarchy. <UnityPackage /> combines the .unitypackage filename and icon into a single styled inline badge. Use it instead of writing `.unitypackage` <UnityPackageIcon />. Save your <UnityPackage /> file somewhere you can find it.

Every page is .mdx (not .md) so React components work inline. Frontmatter sets the sidebar position and title: --- sidebar_position: 2 title: My Page --- Imports go right after the frontmatter block, before any content.

Static images go in static/img/. In markdown prose, use the path as-is: ![alt text](/img/something.png) Inside a React component or JSX, always use useBaseUrl or the path will break in production: import useBaseUrl from '@docusaurus/useBaseUrl'; const src = useBaseUrl('/img/something.png');

Callout boxes for things that need to stand out. Keep them short - one or two sentences max. note note - neutral extra context that's helpful but not critical. Tag: :::note tip tip - shortcuts, recommendations, or things that make life easier. Tag: :::tip info info - background context the reader might not know. Tag: :::info caution caution - things that are easy to get wrong or miss. Also used as a placeholder marker for screenshots still needed. Tag: :::caution warning warning - things that can actually break something if ignored. Tag: :::warning danger danger - use sparingly, only for things with serious consequences. Tag: :::danger

The site CSS is split into six files loaded in dependency order from src/css/custom.css: theme-foundation.css - all --xeno-* CSS custom properties, base html/body rules, scrollbar styling, and text-wrap settings. This is the only place hex values should ever appear. theme-decor.css - the four fixed pseudo-element layers that create the framed decorative border on every page. Appearance is driven entirely by CSS variables, so per-page themes only need to override those variables. theme-docs.css - main content column: doc container background, h1/h2 heading styles, and the rules that hide placeholder markdown headings when a XenoMarkers component immediately follows them. theme-sidebar.css - sidebar shell, category frame cards with rivets, pill labels, the hover-highlight cursor, and the no-frame category modifier. theme-toc.css - right-hand table of contents panel, active cursor indicator, and the previous/next pagination cards. theme-chrome.css - breadcrumbs, navbar, footer (including the rivet decorations at the footer corners), and kbd/abbr overrides.

Each section of the wiki has its own color theme that changes the decorative border layers. Themes are defined in src/theme/shared/xenoPageTheme.ts and applied automatically on navigation - no MDX changes required. Path pattern data-xeno-decor Decor style Notes /docs/troubleshooting troubleshooting alt Yellow/olive palette, alternate mask images /docs/updating updating default Blue/purple palette /docs/customizing/** customizing default Default palette /docs/upload/** upload default Default palette Everything else default default Default warm orange/brown palette To add a new theme, add an entry to PAGE_THEME_DEFINITIONS in xenoPageTheme.ts: { pattern: /\/docs\/my-section(?:\/|$)/, decor: 'my-section', style: 'default', // 'default' or 'alt' - switches the mask image set variables: { '--xeno-page-bg-bottom': '#5ab2f2', '--xeno-page-decor-before-ramp-base': '#113357', '--xeno-page-decor-after-tl': 'rgb(197 220 237)', // ... }, }, style: 'alt' swaps in decor_top_alt.png, decor_bottom_alt.png, and decor_middle_alt.png. Use it if the default mask shapes don't suit the palette. Variable Controls --xeno-page-bg-bottom Bottom color of the full-page background gradient --xeno-page-bg-top Top color of the background gradient (defaults to --xeno-beige-light) --xeno-page-decor-before-ramp-base Base color of the top/bottom mask overlay --xeno-page-decor-before-ramp-highlight Highlight color within the mask overlay --xeno-page-decor-before-opacity Overall opacity of the html::before / body::before layers --xeno-page-decor-before-texture-shadow-blend Blend mode for the texture shadow --xeno-page-decor-after-tl/tr/bl/br Corner radial gradient colors in the center decor layer --xeno-page-decor-after-opacity Overall opacity of the html::after layer --xeno-page-decor-after-texture-blend Blend mode for the center texture layer --xeno-page-decor-after-ramp-base Base color of the ramp highlight layer --xeno-page-decor-after-ramp-highlight Highlight color for the ramp --xeno-page-decor-after-ramp-opacity Multiplied with the layer opacity
A reference for errors you're likely to run into when uploading or using avatars.

Cause: The selected object doesn't have a VRC Avatar Descriptor component, meaning you likely dragged the raw .fbx model instead of the prefab into your hierarchy! Fix: Make sure you put the Prefab into your hierarchy (check Importing the Avatar)

Cause: You might have some dependencies missing or you are on the wrong version of Unity. Fix: Check the Unity Console (Window → General → Console) for any red errors. Fix all script errors before trying to upload. If errors are in third-party packages, try reimporting them via the Creator Companion.

If you get the "VRCFury encountered an error. Failed to build VRCFury component: " error while entering play mode or attempting to upload the model that means you are missing either GoGoLoco or ADJerry's Facetracking Templates while using an older version of the Avatar. Fix: Do one of the following Update the Lucario Avatar (Check Updating) Remove either "FT- Lucario ReUnited UE FaceTracking Prefab" or "GogoLoco Beyond - Lucario ReUnited (VRCFury)" from the avatar in the Hierarchy. (use the images below to figure out which one to delete) GoGoLoco Error VRCFT Error

If your avatar appears as neon pink you most likely are missing the Poiyomi Shaders! Cause: Likely missing shaders Fix: Install Poiyomi using the Installing needed things guide If the shaders still appear as pink even after importing Poiyomi you might need to re-assign the shader as seen in the video below! ▶ Fixing Shaders

documents.t: To update your avatar to the newest version, follow these steps. Check the Avatar Changelog first to see what changed - it's worth knowing before you start, especially if you've made customizations.

New versions are released in the same places as the original - Gumroad, or early on Patreon for supporters. See the home page for all download links. Download the updated .unitypackage file, then import it into your Unity project by double-clicking it or dragging it into the Project window. Unity will show a list of files - leave everything checked and click Import. warning If you edited any of the original files that came with the avatar (painted over a texture, swapped out a mesh, etc.), those changes will be overwritten. Files you created yourself and added separately are safe - Unity only replaces files it recognises from the original package. Before importing, copy anything you want to keep to a folder outside your Unity project. Don't just move it within the project - the import will still overwrite it there.
documents.s: Step 1: Download and import the new package

documents.t: The Blueprint ID is what tells VRChat which avatar slot to update. If it's missing or wrong, your upload will create a brand new avatar instead of replacing the existing one. In the Hierarchy, click the top-level avatar object (the one at the very top, not anything nested inside it). In the Inspector, scroll down until you see a section called Pipeline Manager. Check the Blueprint ID field: If it already has an ID - you're good, skip to Step 3. If it's empty - go to VRChat SDK → Content Manager in the Unity menu bar, find your previously uploaded avatar in the list, and click Copy ID. Paste that into the Blueprint ID field and click Attach. tip Not sure what any of that means? The Uploading page explains the Blueprint ID process in detail.
documents.s: Step 2: Make sure the Blueprint ID matches

documents.t: Once the import is done and the Blueprint ID is confirmed, upload the avatar the same way you did the first time. Head over to the Uploading page if you need a refresher on the steps. tip You don't need to re-enter the name or description. VRChat remembers those from your first upload since you're updating the same avatar, not creating a new one.

If your avatar has a Quest version, make sure you upload that too - otherwise Quest users (including yourself on Quest) will still see the old version. Once you've uploaded for Windows, repeat the process for the Quest version and select Android in the Platform dropdown instead. warning Make sure the Blueprint ID on the Quest prefab matches the PC version! If you need a reminder on how to do that, check the Mobile upload steps.
To get the avatar into Unity you need to import a Unity Package - a .unitypackage file that contains the model, textures, animations, and everything else the avatar needs.

If it's not already open then: Open the Creator Companion and go to the Projects tab. Click Open Project next to your project. Unity will launch, which can take a minute or two. info Unity is slow to open. Just let it load.
documents.s: Step 1 - Open your project in Unity

documents.t: You should have a .unitypackage file from your avatar download, named something like Lucario ReUnited VRC.unitypackage. ⚠️Put a screenshot of the right-click menu here Right-click Menu tip Not sure where it is? Check your Downloads folder, or wherever you saved it after downloading.
There are three ways to do this - pick whichever works for you:

The Project window is the panel at the bottom of Unity that shows all your project files. Inside it, you'll see a folder called Assets in the left sidebar. warning Project window vs Hierarchy These two panels are easy to mix up. The Hierarchy (left side of the screen) shows the objects in your current scene. The Project window (bottom) shows your files on disk. You want the Project window for this step. Right-click the Assets folder. Hover over Import Package. Click Custom Package.... Find your .unitypackage file in the file browser and select it. ▶Video coming soon Right-click Menu tip If the import dialog never appears after doing this, try Option B or Option C below instead.
documents.s: Option A - Right-click the Assets folder

documents.t: Open the folder where your .unitypackage file is saved. Drag the file on top of the Project window in Unity. Drop it anywhere in the panel. ▶Video coming soon Drag and Drop

Find the .unitypackage file in your file explorer. Double-click the .unitypackage. If Unity is open it will pick it up automatically. ▶Video coming soon Double-click Import Whichever method you used, Unity will show a list of everything in the package. Leave everything checked and click Import. caution Put an image of the Import dialog here Wait for the progress bar in the bottom-right corner to finish before doing anything else. info FBX import warnings may appear in the Console after importing. As long as the text is yellow and not red, they are safe to ignore. danger Don't start customizing yet. Do a clean upload first to make sure everything is working correctly before you start making changes. It's much easier to spot problems on a fresh import than after you've already changed things. Head to Uploading once you're done here.

Once the import finishes, navigate to this folder in the Project window: Assets / Monado_Art / Lucario ReUnited VRC / You may also notice a _MekenoTools folder in your Assets. It's a helper package that came with the avatar - just leave it alone, you don't need to touch it. Inside you'll find: The Scene - Double-click to open it. If you're new to Unity this is the easiest starting point since the avatar is already set up inside it. The Prefab - The avatar itself, as a reusable file. The included scene already has both prefabs placed in it, so if you just opened the scene you don't need to drag anything in. There are two versions: Lucario ReUnited PC Prefab - the base version, with the Sir Aaron outfit and mohawk hair on by default. Lucario ReUnited PC Lite Prefab - the same avatar, but with a few things removed to get a better VRChat performance rating (which affects how your avatar looks to others based on their settings). caution Put an image of the Project window showing the folder and files here Once you've opened the scene, the avatar should be visible in the Hierarchy on the left and in the Scene view in the center. You're good to go.
documents.s: Step 4 - Find the scene and prefab

documents.t: Head to Uploading to get the avatar into VRChat before you touch anything.
To get an avatar into VRChat, you'll need to install a few things first. This page walks you through all of it step by step - no prior experience needed.​

danger If you just made your VRChat account, you will need to play the game or AFK in order to increase Trust Rank from Visitor to New User to upload avatars! Making friends can speed this up, or you can get VRC+ to receive New User rank immediately. Trust Ranks
documents.s: Before You Begin - VRChat Trust Rank Requirement

documents.t: The VRChat Creator Companion (usually called VCC) is a free program made by VRChat. Think of it as a control panel that helps you set up everything else. You install it once and it handles the rest. Go to vrchat.com and log in with your VRChat account. Click big blue Download the Creator Companion button. Download the Creator Companion and run the installer like you would any other program.

Unity is the program that actually lets you upload the avatar. VCC will prompt you to install it automatically, so you don't need to go hunting for the right version yourself. Open the Creator Companion. If Unity isn't installed yet, VCC will show a message asking you to install it. Click Install Unity. This opens a program called Unity Hub - it's just a launcher that manages Unity for you. Follow the prompts to finish installing. During setup, you'll be asked to create a free Unity account and activate a Personal license. This is completely free and just lets you use Unity. warning Don't install Unity yourself If you go to the Unity website and download it manually, you'll probably get the wrong version. VRChat is very picky about which version it supports - always let VCC install it for you. caution Already have Unity installed? You might have the wrong version. If you haven't updated VCC or Unity in a while, you may have Unity 2019 installed instead of the required Unity 2022. Using the wrong version will cause your project to break. To fix this: First, make sure your Creator Companion itself is up to date - check for updates and install them if available. Open the Creator Companion and go to Settings in the bottom-left corner. Click the General tab. If you see a pop-up or banner that says something like "Recommended Version Not Installed", click Install Now. Wait for Creator Companion to finish installing the correct version. Once Unity 2022 is installed, you're good to go.

A project is just a folder on your computer where all your avatar files will live. You create and manage it through the Creator Companion. Open the Creator Companion and click Projects in the sidebar on the left. Click the blue Create New Project button in the top right. From the template list, select "Unity 2022 Avatar Project". Give your project a name and choose where to save it. VCC may default to a hidden system folder (Appdata) - somewhere like Documents\VRChat Projects\ is much easier to find later. Click Create and wait for it to finish. This might take a minute or two.

Before you can install anything, VCC needs to know where to find these packages. warning This step is not the same as installing them into Unity. Clicking the buttons below only registers where the packages live. You still need to go through Step 5 to actually put them in your project - don't stop here! Click Add to VCC on each card below. Once you've clicked all four, a message will appear at the bottom telling you what to do next. Mandatory Dependencies VRCFury Automatically sets up complex avatar features so you don't have to do it manually. Add to VCC Didn't work? Go to Settings > Packages > Add Repository and paste: https://vcc.vrcfury.com Poiyomi Toon The shader used for the avatar's materials. Without it, the avatar will appear completely pink. Add to VCC Didn't work? Go to Settings > Packages > Add Repository and paste: https://poiyomi.github.io/vpm/index.json Optional - but heavily recommended ⚠️ These packages are not strictly required, but pay close attention during the upload process. If you choose to skip them, missing packages can produce errors and cause the upload to fail. ADJerry's Face Tracking Templates Adds face tracking support to the avatar. Add to VCC Didn't work? Go to Settings > Packages > Add Repository and paste: https://Adjerry91.github.io/VRCFaceTracking-Templates/index.json GoGoLoco Adds movement options like sitting and laying down anywhere in VRChat. Add to VCC Didn't work? Go to Settings > Packages > Add Repository and paste: https://Spokeek.github.io/goloco/index.json You only need to do this once per package, ever - once a source is added to VCC, it stays there for all future projects.
documents.s: Step 4 - Add the package sources to VCC

documents.t: Now that VCC knows where the packages are, you need to install them into your project. This is the step that puts them in your Unity project and makes them usable. Open Creator Companion and click Projects in the sidebar on the left. Find your project in the list and click Manage Project. You'll see a list of packages. Find each of the following and click the button next to them: VRCFury(Required) - Used to put the avatar together. Poiyomi Toon(Required) - Used for shadersMake sure you pick Toon, not Pro! - Pro is paid and won't work if you don't own it! VRCFT - Jerry's Templates(Optional) - Used for Face Tracking GoGoLoco(Optional) - Used for flight and body poses without FullBody Tracking Wait for VCC to finish installing each one - it may take a moment. info You'll know it worked when the version box changes from none to a version number (e.g. 1.2.3), and the button changes to .
documents.s: Step 5 - Install the packages into your project

documents.t: Once everything is installed, head to Unity Basics to learn how to navigate Unity or skip to Uploading if you are already familiar with Unity!

tip Already know Unity? If you've used Unity before and feel comfortable navigating it, feel free to skip straight to Importing the Avatar. When you open your project for the first time, Unity can look pretty overwhelming. There are panels everywhere and none of it is obvious. This page breaks down what each part of the screen does so you're not flying blind.

Open the Creator Companion and go to the Projects tab. Click Open Project next to your project. Unity will launch, which can take a minute or two. info Unity takes a while to open, especially on first launch. This is normal - just let it finish. warning Unity does not autosave. Press Ctrl+S regularly to save your scene. If you close Unity without saving, any changes you made will be gone.

When Unity first opens, you'll see something like this: Unity Editor Layout Each section is its own panel, and you can resize or rearrange them. Don't worry if yours looks slightly different - Unity lets you move things around. info What's a scene? A scene is what's currently loaded and active in your project. Think of it like a stage - your project folder holds all your files, and the scene is what's actually set up and ready to work with. The avatar lives inside a scene, and you'll need to open the right one before you can upload it.

Where: Top-left panel. Hierarchy Hierarchy Panel The Hierarchy is a list of everything that exists in your current scene. Think of it like a folder tree - objects can be nested inside other objects. For avatar work, this is where you'll find your avatar. It will usually appear as a single entry that you can click the arrow next to expand and see all its parts (bones, meshes, etc.). tip When you click something in the Hierarchy, it gets selected and its details show up in the Inspector on the right. ▶ Hierarchy - Inspector Link

Where: Right-side panel. Inspector Inspector Panel The Inspector shows you the details of whatever you have selected. If you click on your avatar in the Hierarchy, the Inspector will show all the components attached to it - things like the Avatar Descriptor (which tells VRChat this is an avatar) and any other settings. You'll interact with the Inspector a lot when following guides, since most settings are changed here. If it shows something unexpected you probably clicked the wrong thing - go back to the Hierarchy and click what you wanted. If it goes blank, nothing is selected.

tip You can lock the inspector by pressing the little padlock icon in the top right corner of the Inspector window. Locking the inspector will prevent it from changing when you select other things or deselect everything altogether. Padlock location

You can add more Inspector panels (or any panels for that matter) if you need to. To do so Right-Click the Inspector tab and click "Add Tab/Inspector" ▶ Adding and Locking Inspectors tip You can combine this with locking to have different Inspectors showing you different things if you need to quickly edit a number of things!

Where: Large panel in the center. Scene Scene View The Scene View is a 3D viewport where you can see and move around the assets currently present in the Hierarchy visually. You can think of it like a free camera flying around your scene.

Right-click + drag - Rotate the camera Middle-click + drag - Pan the camera Scroll wheel - Zoom in/out Press F (with something selected) - Focus the camera on that object ▶ Scene view - Basic Controls

Right-click + WASD - Fly through the scene (hold right-click, then move with WASD) Right-click + Q/E - Move the camera down/up while flying Right-click + Scroll Wheel Up/Down - Change the camera speed Right-click + WASD + Shift - Fly faster ▶ Scene view - Fly Controls For uploading, you don't really need to move things around in the Scene View - just knowing how to navigate it is enough.

If you select an object and see colored arrows or handles appear on it, you've activated a transform tool. W, E, and R switch between Move, Rotate, and Scale. If you accidentally nudge something, Ctrl+Z will undo it. ▶ Scene view - Inspector Link tip Clicking something in the Scene view selects it, just like clicking in the Hierarchy - and its details will show up in the Inspector on the right.

Where: Usually tabbed next to the Scene View (click the "Game" tab to switch). Game View The Game View shows what the camera inside the scene sees - basically a preview of what things would look like in-game. For avatar uploading you won't use this much. danger Entering play mode switches to this tab automatically. To get back to the Scene view, press the Scene tab next to the Game tab. More importantly - any changes you make while in play mode are discarded when you stop it. If you tweak something and it looks right, stop play mode first, then make the change for real.

Where: Bottom panel. Project Project Window The Project window is your file browser. It shows all the files that make up your project - textures, materials, scripts, prefabs, and so on. Think of it like File Explorer, but only showing the contents of your project folder. When you import your avatar files, they'll appear here. You can double-click folders to open them, and drag files from the Project window into the Hierarchy to add them to your scene. note Dragging onto the Scene view instead places the object wherever the camera is looking, not at the center of the world. ▶ Project - Hierarchy Drag

Where: Usually tabbed next to the Project window (click "Console" to switch). Console The Console shows messages from Unity - information, warnings, and errors. White messages - General info, usually safe to ignore. Yellow messages - Warnings. Often harmless, but worth noting. Red messages - Errors. These are usually safe to ignore unless they prevent you from entering play mode or building the avatar. If your upload fails or something breaks, the Console is the first place to check. note If you see a wall of red errors when you first open your project, don't panic. Make sure all mandatory packages from the Installation step are properly installed - missing packages are the most common cause.

Where: Very top of the window. Toolbar The menu bar at the top works like any other program. The one you'll use most is VRChat SDK, which is where you open the upload panel. tip If you accidentally drag panels around and can't get back to a normal layout, go to Window → Layouts → Default to reset everything.
Now that you know your way around, head to Importing the Avatar to continue.
Make sure you've completed the Installation steps before continuing. Outfits and customization are covered in the Customizing section.

In Unity, go to the top menu bar and click VRChat SDK → Show Control Panel. caution Put an image of where to find it If you don't see this menu, the SDK probably isn't installed correctly - go back to the Creator Companion and make sure the VRChat SDK package is added to your project.

In the SDK window, go to the Authentication tab and sign in with your VRChat account. If prompted for a two-factor authentication code, check your email. tip Sign in with your email address, not your username. Username logins don't tend to work as reliably in the SDK.

Switch to the Builder tab at the top of the SDK window. In the Selected Avatar dropdown, choose your avatar. If the dropdown is empty, make sure the avatar's scene is open and the avatar is in the Hierarchy. The SDK will run a few checks. Any errors shown in red will have a button next to them to fix them automatically - click it and continue. Warnings in yellow are usually safe to ignore.

Fill in the Avatar Name and give it a Thumbnail - click Select Image to use an image file, or Capture in Scene to take a screenshot from the Scene view. Description and tags are optional. Make sure Build & Publish your Avatar Online is selected as the Build Type and Windows is selected in the Platform dropdown. Click Build & Publish. Wait for Unity to finish building. This can take anywhere from a few minutes to upward of 20 - Unity may look frozen during this time, which is normal. Don't close it. If successful, you'll see Build Successful in green text in the SDK panel. Your avatar will appear in VRChat under My Avatars.

If you want Quest users to see your avatar when you're on PC (and vice versa), you need to upload a mobile version and link it to the same avatar slot. info What's a Blueprint ID? It's VRChat's internal ID for an avatar slot. Linking both versions to the same ID means they count as one avatar. If you skip this, they'll be treated as two completely separate uploads and cross-platform visibility won't work. Find the prefab for the Mobile version and drag it into the Hierarchy. In the SDK's Content Manager tab, find your uploaded PC avatar and click Copy ID. In the Hierarchy, click the top-level object of the Quest avatar - the one at the very top, not any of the things nested inside it. In the Inspector, scroll down until you see a section called Pipeline Manager. Paste the copied ID into the Blueprint ID field and click Attach. Repeat the upload steps above with Android selected in the Platform dropdown.
If your build fails, the SDK throws an error you can't auto-fix, or the avatar doesn't appear in VRChat after uploading, check the Troubleshooting page for common errors and fixes.
Nice work! Head over to the Customizing section whenever you're ready to start on outfits and accessories.
